Red-tailed sportive lemur (Lepilemur ruficaudatus) neonates enter the world at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 27 grams [Wwb = 27 grams], a figure inferred from measurements of the congeneric species Lepilemur mustelinus. This altricial newborn is entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial weeks of life, clinging to the mother's ventral fur while she forages nocturnally. The gestation period, defined as the age at birth, lasts approximately 136 days [tg = approximately 136 days] when the mother's core body temperature is maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], a thermal regime typical of resting lepilemurids. This relatively lengthy gestation for a primate of this body size is thought to reflect the slow metabolic pace characteristic of folivorous strepsirrhines. Following parturition, the neonate undergoes a period of rapid physical development, though it remains inside the maternal home range for several weeks before beginning to explore its surroundings independently.

The species exhibits a conservative reproductive strategy, with females giving birth to an average of one pup per litter [N_R_i = one pup per litter] and producing a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. This annual reproductive output, with the maximum reproductive rate resulting in just one offspring per year, is tightly linked to the pronounced seasonal availability of young leaves in their dry deciduous forest habitat in western Madagascar. The timing of parturition is synchronized with the rainy season, when food resources are most abundant, ensuring that the energy demands of lactation coincide with peak nutritional quality. Maternal investment is substantial, as the single offspring requires prolonged care and provisioning. The energetic costs of gestation and lactation are considerable for a mammal of this size, and the slow life history is further reflected in the prolonged period of juvenile development. Weaning occurs when the infant has reached a wet weight of approximately 200 grams [Wwx = approximately 200 grams], a threshold also derived from observations of Lepilemur mustelinus, marking the point at which the young begin to consume solid foliage.

Juveniles undergo a protracted period of growth before attaining adult body proportions, with the ultimate wet weight of an adult individual reaching approximately 800 grams [Wwi = approximately 800 grams]. This asymptotic mass is modest compared to many other lemurids but is consistent with the highly specialized folivorous diet that limits caloric intake. The time since birth at weaning, a key developmental milestone, is recorded at approximately 85 days since birth [tx = approximately 85 days since birth] under conditions where maternal body temperature is maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], based on comparable data from Lepilemur mustelinus. After achieving nutritional independence, the young animal continues to refine its foraging skills and expand its home range. Growth rates during the post-weaning period are gradual, reflecting the challenges of extracting sufficient energy from a leaf-based diet. Adult body mass is typically reached after several years of steady growth, and the species' slow metabolic rate likely contributes to this extended developmental timeline.

Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs relatively late in life for a mammal of this size. The time since birth at puberty is approximately 595 days since birth [tp = approximately 595 days since birth] when the individual's core temperature is maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], a thermal condition that is typical during inactive periods. This delayed sexual maturation is a hallmark of the genus Lepilemur and is thought to be an adaptation to the unpredictable resource availability of their dry forest environment. The extended juvenile period allows ample time for the development of complex social and spatial cognition, as well as the establishment of a personal home range. Following the attainment of puberty, young adults may not breed immediately, as competition for high-quality territories can delay first reproduction further. The species' overall life history strategy is K-selected, prioritizing survival and prolonged development over rapid, high-volume reproduction. This pattern is consistent with the demographic pressures faced by small-bodied primates in seasonal habitats.

Longevity records for the red-tailed sportive lemur indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 13,213 days [am = approximately 13,213 days] when the individual is maintained at a stable core body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], which translates to just over 36 years. This remarkable lifespan, verified through long-term field studies of marked individuals, is among the highest recorded for a small-bodied folivorous primate. The species' maximum basal metabolic rate, measured as an oxygen consumption of 225 milliliters per hour [JOi = 225 milliliters per hour] at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], is notably low for a mammal of its size, reflecting its energetically conservative lifestyle. This reduced metabolic expenditure is an adaptation to the low-quality, high-fiber diet of leaves, which provides limited digestible energy. The combination of a low metabolic rate, a late age at first reproduction, and an extraordinarily long lifespan positions Lepilemur ruficaudatus as a textbook example of a slow life history strategy, where the emphasis is placed on individual survival and the steady accumulation of reproductive opportunities over many years.
